newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH SAYS SPORT IS DIVIDED IN DRUG BATTLE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH SAYS SPORT IS DIVIDED IN DRUG BATTLE.

text.p: International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Juan Antonio Samaranch accused on Tuesday some sporting organisations of "doing nothing" to catch drug cheats.
Samaranch said there was a split in international sport between officials who wanted to catch doping offenders and those who did not.
"I am surprised with sports that there are two different worlds," Samaranch said in an interview. "One world with the IOC and international federations fighting against doping.
"There is a second world where they do nothing against doping."
The IOC chief would not give the names of the countries or federations to which he was referring.
His comments may have been aimed partly at the United States where some professional sports are not so tough as athletics with their testing and penalties.
Samaranch praised athletics for having one of the most stringent anti-doping programmes, especially through its out-of-competition tests.

But he said it was often a hard task for organisers of events to be tough on drugs, referring to the recent Pan-Arab Games in Beirut which were tainted by drug abuse with the disqualification of 12 athletes.
It was the first time athletes had been thrown out for drug use since the inaugural Games in Egypt in 1953.

"Look at the Pan-Arab Games in Beirut. For the first time they had doping control with the help of the IOC and they got more than nine athletes," Samaranch said. "But they got a lot of critics saying the event was full of doping.
"They have had five or so games before and they have not had a single word against the games. It can be discouraging for organisers to fight."

Samaranch, who met International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) chief Primo Nebiolo before the start of the Athens world championships, said he was hopeful of finding a solution to their dispute over money from the Olympic Games.
Nebiolo wants serious talks with the IOC about improving the share of the revenue given to athletics -- the showcase of the Games -- after Samaranch has stood for re-election next month.
"The IAAF is getting much more money from (the 2000 games in) Sydney," Samaranch said. "I am sure we can find a solution. We will speak about this next year. We have time."
Nebiolo said earlier this week that athletics received just $8 million from the Olympics while it made $100 million from the world championships.

The IOC recently signed a television deal with the American network NBC worth more than $2 billion. The contract which the IOC has with its leading sponsors is worth around $400 million over four years.
